entries.83bd1317529953da37ea360501b9e8b9b98cddb3: <div sID="gen4355" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Josh.12" sID="Josh.12"/> <div eID="gen4355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4356" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a summary of Israel's conquests. I. Their conquests under Moses, on the other side Jordan (for we now suppose ourselves in Canaan) eastward, which we had the history of, <reference osisRef="Num.21.24-Num.21.35">Num. xxi. 24</reference>, &c. And here the abridgment of that history, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.1-Josh.12.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. Their conquests under Joshua, on this side Jordan, westward. 1. The country they reduced, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.7-Josh.12.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. 2. The kings they subdued, thirty-one in all, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.9-Josh.12.24">ver. 9-24</reference>. And this comes in here, not only as a conclusion of the history of the wars of Canaan (that we might at one view see what they had got), but as a preface to the history of the dividing of Canaan, that all that might be put together which they were not to make a distribution of.
entries.009b38aa4fe73b69ee6bbbb787d77d78d6f7f89c: <div eID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4356" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Summary of Israel's Conquests. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4358" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the kings of the land, which the children of Israel smote, and possessed their land on the other side Jordan toward the rising of the sun, from the river Arnon unto mount Hermon, and all the plain on the east: <hi type="super">2</hi> Sihon king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon, <hi type="italic">and</hi> ruled from Aroer, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the bank of the river Arnon, and from the middle of the river, and from half Gilead, even unto the river Jabbok, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> the border of the children of Ammon; <hi type="super">3</hi> And from the plain to the sea of Chinneroth on the east, and unto the sea of the plain, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the salt sea on the east, the way to Beth-jeshimoth; and from the south, under Ashdoth-pisgah: <hi type="super">4</hi> And the coast of Og king of Bashan, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> of the remnant of the giants, that dwelt at Ashtaroth and at Edrei, <hi type="super">5</hi> And reigned in mount Hermon, and in Salcah, and in all Bashan, unto the border of the Geshurites and the Maachathites, and half Gilead, the border of Sihon king of Heshbon. <hi type="super">6</hi> Them did Moses the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and the children of Israel smite: and Moses the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> gave it <hi type="italic">for</hi> a possession unto the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh. <div eID="gen4358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4359" type="x-p"/> Joshua, or whoever else is the historian before he comes to sum up the new conquests Israel had made, in these verses receives their former conquests in Moses's time, under whom they became masters of the great and potent kingdoms of Sihon and Og. Note, Fresh mercies must not drown the remembrance of former mercies, nor must the glory of the present instruments of good to the church be suffered to eclipse and diminish the just honour of those who have gone before them, and who were the blessings and ornaments of their day. Joshua's services and achievements are confessedly great, but let not those under Moses be overlooked and forgotten, since God was the same who wrought both, and both put together proclaim him the Alpha and Omega of Israel's great salvation. Here is, 1. A description of this conquered country, the measure and bounds of it in general (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">From the river Arnon</hi> in the south, to <hi type="italic">Mount Hermon</hi> in the north. In particular, here is a description of the kingdom of Sihon (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.2-Josh.12.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), and that of Og, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.4-Josh.12.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Moses had described this country very particularly (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">Deut. ii. 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">iii. 4</reference>, &c.), and this description here agrees with his. King Og is said to dwell at Ashtaroth and Edrei (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.4">v. 4</reference>), probably because they were both his royal cities; he had palaces in both, and resided sometimes in one and sometimes in the other; one perhaps was his summer seat and the other his winter seat. But Israel took both from him, and made one grave to serve him that could not be content with one palace. 2. The distribution of this country. Moses assigned it to the two tribes and a half, at their request, and divided it among them (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.6">v. 6</reference>), of which we had the story at large, <reference osisRef="Num.32.1-Num.32.42">Num. xxxii</reference>. The dividing of it when it was conquered by Moses is here mentioned as an example to Joshua what he must do now that he had conquered the country on this side Jordan. Moses, in his time, gave to one part of Israel a very rich and fruitful country, but it was on the outside of Jordan; but Joshua gave to all Israel the holy land, the mountain of God's sanctuary, within Jordan: so the law conferred upon some few of God's spiritual Israel external temporal blessings, which were earnests of good things to come; but our Lord Jesus, the true Joshua, has provided for all the children of promise spiritual blessings—the privileges of the sanctuary, and the heavenly Canaan. The triumphs and grants of the law were glorious, but those of the gospel far exceed in glory.
entries.5cee88d03bd47809b99522ea2ec07d53c7715046: <div eID="gen4359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4360" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the kings of the country which Joshua and the children of Israel smote on this side Jordan on the west, from Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon even unto the mount Halak, that goeth up to Seir; which Joshua gave unto the tribes of Israel <hi type="italic">for</hi> a possession according to their divisions; <hi type="super">8</hi> In the mountains, and in the valleys, and in the plains, and in the springs, and in the wilderness, and in the south country; the Hittites, the Amorites, and the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites: <hi type="super">9</hi> The king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> beside Beth-el, one; <hi type="super">10</hi> The king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; <hi type="super">11</hi> The king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; <hi type="super">12</hi> The king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one; <hi type="super">13</hi> The king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one; <hi type="super">14</hi> The king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one; <hi type="super">15</hi> The king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one; <hi type="super">16</hi> The king of Makkedah, one; the king of Beth-el, one; <hi type="super">17</hi> The king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; <hi type="super">18</hi> The king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; <hi type="super">19</hi> The king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one; <hi type="super">20</hi> The king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one; <hi type="super">21</hi> The king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; <hi type="super">22</hi> The king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam of Carmel, one; <hi type="super">23</hi> The king of Dor in the coast of Dor, one; the king of the nations of Gilgal, one; <hi type="super">24</hi> The king of Tirzah, one: all the kings thirty and one. <div eID="gen4360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4361" type="x-p"/> We have here a breviate of Joshua's conquests. <div eID="gen4361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4362" type="x-p"/> I. The limits of the country he conquered. It lay between Jordan on the east and the Mediterranean Sea on the west, and extended from Baal-gad near Lebanon in the north to Halak, which lay upon the country of Edom in the south, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.7">v. 7</reference>. The boundaries are more largely described, <reference osisRef="Num.34.2-Num.34.12">Num. xxxiv. 2</reference>, &c. But what is here said is enough to show that God had been as good as his word, and had given them possession of all he had promised them by Moses, if they would but have kept it. <div eID="gen4362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4363" type="x-p"/> II. The various kinds of land that were found in this country, which contributed both to its pleasantness and to its fruitfulness, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.8">v. 8</reference>. There were mountains, not craggy, and rocky, and barren, which are frightful to the traveller and useless to the inhabitants, but fruitful hills, such as put forth <hi type="italic">precious things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.15">Deut. xxxiii. 15</reference>), which charmed the spectator's eye and filled the owner's hand. And valleys, not mossy and boggy, but <hi type="italic">covered with corn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.13">Ps. lxv. 13</reference>. There were plains, and springs to water them; and even in that rich land there were wildernesses too, or forests, which were not so thickly inhabited as other parts, yet had towns and houses in them, but served as foils to set off the more pleasant and fruitful countries. <div eID="gen4363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4364" type="x-p"/> III. The several nations that had been in possession of this country—Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, &c., all of them descended from Canaan, the accursed son of Ham, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.15-Gen.10.18">Gen. x. 15-18</reference>. Seven nations they are called (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deut. vii. 1</reference>), and so many are there reckoned up, but here six only are mentioned, the Girgashites being either lost or left out, though we find them, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.16">Gen. x. 16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.15.21">xv. 21</reference>. Either they were incorporated with some other of these nations, or, as the tradition of the Jews is, upon the approach of Israel under Joshua they all withdrew and went into Africa, leaving their country to be possessed by Israel, with whom they saw it was to no purpose to contend, and therefore they are not named among the nations that Joshua subdued. <div eID="gen4364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4365" type="x-p"/> IV. A list of the kings that were conquered and subdued by the sword of Israel, some in the field, others in their own cities, thirty-one in all, and very particularly named and counted, it should seem, in the order in which they were conquered; for the catalogue begins with the kings of Jericho and Ai, then takes in the king of Jerusalem and the princes of the south that were in confederacy with him, and then proceeds to those of the northern association. Now, 1. This shows what a very fruitful country Canaan then was, which could support so many kingdoms, and in which so many kings chose to throng together rather than disperse themselves into other countries, which we may suppose not yet inhabited, but where, though they might find more room, they could not expect such plenty and pleasure: this was the land God spied out for Israel; and yet at this day it is one of the most barren, despicable, and unprofitable countries in the world: such is the effect of the curse it lies under, since its possessors rejected Christ and his gospel, as was foretold by Moses, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deut. xxix. 23</reference>. 2. It shows what narrow limits men's ambition was then confined to. These kings contented themselves with the government, each of them, of one city and the towns and villages that pertained to it; and no one of them, for aught that appears, aimed to make himself master of the rest, but, when there was occasion, all united for the common safety. Yet it should seem that what was wanting in the extent of their territories was made up in the absoluteness of their power, their subjects being all their tenants and vassals, and entirely at their command. 3. It shows how good God was to Israel, in giving them victory over all these kings, and possession of all these kingdoms, and what obligations he hereby laid upon them to <hi type="italic">observe his statutes and to keep his laws,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.44-Ps.105.45">Ps. cv. 44, 45</reference>. Here were thirty-one kingdoms, or seigniories, to be divided among nine tribes and a half of Israel. Of these there fell to the lot of Judah the kingdoms of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Debir, Arad, Libnah, and Adullam, eight in all, besides part of the kingdom of Jerusalem and part of Geder. Benjamin had the kingdoms of Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Makkedah, Beth-el, and the nations of Gilgal, six in all. Simeon had the kingdom of Hormah and part of Geder. Ephraim had the kingdoms of Gezer and Tirzah. Manasseh (that half-tribe) had the kingdoms of Tappuah and Hepher, Taanach and Megiddo. Asher had the kingdoms of Aphek and Achshaph. Zebulun had the kingdoms of Lasharon, Shimron-meron, and Jokneam. Naphtali had the kingdoms of Madon, Hazor, and Kedesh. And Issachar had that of Dor. These were some of the great and famous kings that God smote, <hi type="italic">for his mercy endureth for ever; and gave their land for a heritage, even a heritage unto Israel his servant, for his mercy endureth for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.136.17-Ps.136.24">Ps. cxxxvi. 17</reference>, &c.  <chapter eID="Josh.12"/> <div eID="gen4365" type="x-p"/>

entries.c7661280aed928edd7c524fed71691e40204fa09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2102"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.12.1-Josh.12.6">Jos 12:1-6</reference>. The Two Kings Whose Countries Moses Took and Disposed of.</title> <div sID="gen2820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2102"/><hi type="bold">1. Now these are the kings of the land, which the children of Israel smote, and possessed their land on the other side Jordan--</hi>This chapter contains a recapitulation of the conquests made in the promised land, with the additional mention of some places not formerly noted in the sacred history. The river Arnon on the south and mount Hermon on the north were the respective boundaries of the land acquired by the Israelites beyond Jordan (see <reference osisRef="Num.21.21-Num.21.24">Nu 21:21-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">De 2:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3-2Cor.3.16">3:3-16</reference> [and see on De 2:24]). <div eID="gen2820" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3c34822e8b705b0efafa7ddd340b6015e8e07e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2103"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.12.7-Josh.12.24">Jos 12:7-24</reference>. The One and Thirty Kings on the West Side of Jordan, Which Joshua Smote.</title> <div sID="gen2821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2103"/><hi type="bold">7. Baal-gad ... even unto ... Halak--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Josh.11.17">Jos 11:17</reference>). A list of thirty-one chief towns is here given; and, as the whole land contained a superficial extent of only fifteen miles in length by fifty in breadth, it is evident that these capital cities belonged to petty and insignificant kingdoms. With a few exceptions, they were not the scenes of any important events recorded in the sacred history, and therefore do not require a particular notice. <chapter eID="Josh.12"/>

entries.07ec4fa38b7c2eddeb35f5cdc6608d3f24c2f2f0: <div eID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7851" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7852" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7852" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7851" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7853" type="x-p"/> A list of the kings on the east of Jordan, which were conquered by Moses, with their territories, <reference osisRef="Jos.12.1-Jos.12.6">Jos 12:1-6</reference>. A list of those on the west side of Jordan, conquered by Joshua, in number thirty-one, vv. 7-24. <div eID="gen7853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7855" type="x-p"/> From the river Arnon unto Mount Hermon - Arnon was the boundary of all the southern coast of the land occupied by the Israelites beyond Jordan; and the mountains of Hermon were the boundaries on the north. Arnon takes its rise in the mountains of Gilead, and having run a long way from north to south falls into the Dead Sea, near the same place into which Jordan discharges itself. <div eID="gen7855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7856" type="x-p"/> And all the plain on the east - All the land from the plains of Moab to Mount Hermon.
entries.778713ab42d581184c764d5f8e5433b63d96e07f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7857" type="x-p"/> From Aroer - Aroer was situated on the western side of the river Arnon, in the middle of the valley through which this river takes its course. The kingdom of Sihon extended from the river Arnon and the city of Aroer on the south to the river Jabbok on the north. <div eID="gen7857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7858" type="x-p"/> And from half Gilead - The mountains of Gilead extended from north to south from Mount Hermon towards the source of the river Arnon, which was about the midst of the extent of the kingdom of Sihon: thus Sihon is said to have possessed the half of Gilead, that is, the half of the mountains and of the country which bore the name of Gilead on the east of his territories. <div eID="gen7858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7859" type="x-p"/> River Jabbok - This river has its source in the mountains of Gilead; and, running from east to west, falls into Jordan. It bounds the territories of Sihon on the north, and those of the Ammonites on the south.
entries.48f26ee25a77558b95345bd0c3fb41ce90a6734b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7860" type="x-p"/> The sea of Chinneroth - Or Gennesareth, the same as the lake or sea of Tiberias. <div eID="gen7860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7861" type="x-p"/> The Salt Sea on the east - ים המלח yam hammelach, which is here translated the Salt Sea, is understood by others to mean the sea of the city Melach. Where can we find any thing that can be called a salt sea on the east of the lake of Gennesareth? Some think that the lake Asphaltites, called also the Dead Sea, Sea of the Desert, Sea of Sodom, and Salt Sea, is here intended. <div eID="gen7861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7862" type="x-p"/> Beth-jeshimoth - A city near the Dead Sea in the plains of Moab. <div eID="gen7862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7863" type="x-p"/> Ashdoth-pisgah - Supposed to be a city at the foot of Mount Pisgah.
entries.9e0171f3bb4006b8c479dc1f5081b399b77fa030: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7864" type="x-p"/> Coast of Og king of Bashan - Concerning this person see the notes on <reference osisRef="Deu.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Num.21.35">Num 21:35</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen7864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7865" type="x-p"/> The remnant or the giants - Or, Rephaim. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">Gen 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deu.2.7">Deu 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.11">Deu 2:11</reference>.
entries.64b3271546cf3e9696187e4a68d26598869cad61: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7866" type="x-p"/> The border of the Geshurites - The country of Bashan, in the days of Moses and Joshua, extended from the river Jabbok on the south to the frontiers of the Geshurites and Maachathites on the north, to the foot of the mountains of Hermon.
entries.15d99d577138f094d88b864adaa87d3e14d9874e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen7866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7867" type="x-p"/> From Baal-gad - A repetition of what is mentioned <reference osisRef="Jos.11.17">Jos 11:17</reference>.
entries.b88d6fa0a48ec62989b1c90a6473f13b777b3ba6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7868" type="x-p"/> The king of Jericho, etc. - On this and the following verses see the notes on <reference osisRef="Jos.10.1-Jos.10.3">Jos 10:1-3</reference> (note).
entries.8dfc8bb66a1f06ded0f2455f5ef0d16307331507: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen7868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7869" type="x-p"/> The king of Geder - Probably the same with Gedor, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.58">Jos 15:58</reference>; it was situated in the tribe of Judah.
entries.7ef250c6d37524de9a9269ecc7b2e4b69e02d672: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen7869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7870" type="x-p"/> The king of Hormah - Supposed to be the place where the Israelites were defeated by the Canaanites see <reference osisRef="Num.14.45">Num 14:45</reference>; and which probably was called Hormah, הרמה chormah, or destruction, from this circumstance.
entries.dc8a0202e187a9a7a6def11af47113dbc4f3c681: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen7870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7871" type="x-p"/> Adullam - A city belonging to the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>. In a cave at this place David often secreted himself during his persecution by Saul; <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1">1Sam 22:1</reference>.
entries.e58458bb8a1cf8c5e17283d0733a568f871233b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen7871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7872" type="x-p"/> Tappuah - There were two places of this name: one in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.34">Jos 15:34</reference>, and another in the tribe of Ephraim on the borders of Manasseh; but which of the two is meant here cannot be ascertained. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.15.53">Jos 15:53</reference>. <div eID="gen7872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7873" type="x-p"/> Hepher - The same, according to Calmet, as Ophrah in the tribe of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.23">Jos 18:23</reference>.
entries.9ad036ee4916214e248e1a860e88ac3032308acf: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen7873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7874" type="x-p"/> Aphek - There were several cities of this name: one in the tribe of Asher, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.30">Jos 19:30</reference>, another in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1">1Sam 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sam 29:1</reference>; and a third in Syria, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.26">1Kgs 20:26</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.17">2Kgs 13:17</reference>. Which of the two former is here intended cannot be ascertained. <div eID="gen7874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7875" type="x-p"/> Lasharon - There is no city of this name known. Some consider the ל lamed in the word לשרון lashsharon to be the sign of the genitive case, and in this sense it appears to have been understood by the Vulgate, which translates rex Saron, the king of Sharon. This was rather a district than a city, and is celebrated in the Scriptures for its fertility; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Isa 33:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Isa 35:2</reference>. Some suppose it was the same with Saron, near Lydda, mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.9.35">Act 9:35</reference>.
entries.9978e2d0b9f00f41e3e4d7e24a8b811c9f0db8b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen7875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> Shimron-meron - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference> (note).
entries.85b75af2ff78796ed8418941f79252b3a6b976aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> Taanach - A city in the half tribe of Manasseh, to the west of Jordan, not far from the frontiers of Zebulun, <reference osisRef="Jos.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>. This city was assigned to the Levites, <reference osisRef="Jos.21.25">Jos 21:25</reference>.
entries.7ebf644f6b8f7d38f49bae038d1193704e04e5a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> Kedesh - There was a city of this name in the tribe of Naphtali, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.37">Jos 19:37</reference>. It was given to the Levites, and was one of the cities of refuge, <reference osisRef="Jos.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>. <div eID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> Jokneam of Carmel - This city is said to have been at the foot of Mount Carmel, near the river Belus, in the tribe of Zebulun, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.11">Jos 19:11</reference>. It was given to the Levites, <reference osisRef="Jos.21.34">Jos 21:34</reference>.
entries.a604094e872b500ff36344cd4d5fb5f2e28702c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7880" type="x-p"/> The king of Dor - The city of this name fell to the lot of the children of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Jos.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>. Bochart observes that it was one of the oldest royal cities in Phoenicia. The Canaanites held it, <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.27">Jdg 1:27</reference>. Antiochus Sydetes besieged it in aftertimes, but could not make himself master of it. See Bochart, Canaan, lib. i., c. 28, and Dodd. <div eID="gen7880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> The king of the nations of Gilgal - This is supposed to mean the higher Galilee, surnamed Galilee of the Gentiles or, nations, as the Hebrew word גוים goyim means. On this ground it should be read king of Galilee of the nations. Others suppose it is the same country with that of which Tidal was king, see <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen 14:1</reference>. The place is very uncertain, and commentators have rendered it more so by their conjectures.
entries.e52906736f15d07b1e0a4006d2ff0c9f3d5deccb: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> King of Tirzah - This city appears to have been for a long time the capital of the kingdom of Israel, and the residence of its kings. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.17">1Kgs 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.21">1Kgs 15:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.33">1Kgs 15:33</reference>. Its situation cannot be exactly ascertained; but it is supposed to have been situated on a mountain about three leagues south of Samaria. <div eID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7883" type="x-p"/> All the kings thirty and one - The Septuagint say εικοσι εννεα, twenty-nine, and yet set down but twenty-eight, as they confound or omit the kings of Beth-el, Lasharon, and Madon. <div eID="gen7883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> So many kings in so small a territory, shows that their kingdoms must have been very small indeed. The kings of Beth-el and Ai had but about 12,000 subjects in the whole; but in ancient times all kings had very small territories. Every village or town had its chief; and this chief was independent of his neighbors, and exercised regal power in his own district. In reading all ancient histories, as well as the Bible, this circumstance must be kept constantly in view; for we ought to consider that in those times both kings and kingdoms were but a faint resemblance of those now. <div eID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7885" type="x-p"/> Great Britain, in ancient times, was divided into many kingdoms: in the time of the Saxons it was divided into seven, hence called the Saxon heptarchy. But when Julius Caesar first entered this island, he found four kings in Kent alone; Cingetorix, Carnilius, Taximagulus, and Segonax. Hence we need not wonder at the numbers we read of in the land of Canaan. Ancient Gaul was thus divided; and the great number of sovereign princes, secular bishops, landgraves, dukes, etc., etc., in Germany, are the modern remains of those ancient divisions.  <chapter eID="Josh.12"/> <div eID="gen7885" type="x-p"/>

entries.9c651ea4ed5dae9e7bac301da9fbb0801005b871: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.1">Jos 12:1</reference> <div eID="gen2827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2828" type="x-p"/> List of the <hi type="italic">kings</hi> whom the Israelites smote, and whose land they took, <hi type="italic">on the other side of the Jordan</hi>, - namely, the land by the brook Arnon (Mojeb; see Num 21:13) to Hermon (Jebel es Sheikh, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.8">Deu 3:8</reference>), and the whole of the eastern Arabah (the valley of the Jordan on the eastern side of the river).
entries.6a83a9e2fed03fc13beb355b10992a1acb336c9d: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.2-Josh.12.3">Jos 12:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen2828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2829" type="x-p"/> On Sihon and his kingdom, see Num 21:24; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">Deu 2:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.16">Deu 3:16</reference>-17. “<hi type="italic">Aroër on the Arnon</hi>:” the present ruins of <hi type="italic">Araayr</hi>, on the northern bank of the Mojeb (see Num 32:34). הנּחל ותוך, “<hi type="italic">and</hi> (from) <hi type="italic">the middle of the valley onwards</hi>:” i.e., according to the parallel passages in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.9">Jos 13:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16">Jos 13:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">Deu 2:36</reference>, from the town in the Arnon valley, the city of Moab mentioned in Num 22:36, viz., <hi type="italic">Ar</hi> or <hi type="italic">Areopolis</hi> (see at Num 21:15) in the neighbourhood of Aroër, which is mentioned as the exclusive <hi type="italic">terminus a quo</hi> of the land taken by the Israelites along with the inclusive terminus Aroër. “<hi type="italic">Half-Gilead</hi>,” i.e., the mountainous district on the south side of the Jabbok (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference>), “<hi type="italic">to the river Jabbok</hi>,” i.e., the upper Jabbok, the present Nahr Ammân (see at Num 21:24).
entries.7021e6fa618eceb3e7ff3837feeefca6e36f2a39: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.4-Josh.12.5">Jos 12:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen2830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2831" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And the territory of Og</hi>,” sc., they took possession of (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.1">Jos 12:1</reference>). On Og, vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference>; and on his residences, <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi> (probably to be seen in Tell Ashtereh) and <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi> (now <hi type="italic">Draa</hi> or <hi type="italic">Dêra</hi>), see at <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference> and Num 21:33. On his territory, see <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>-14.
entries.3f4f45118d904da05c3fca53438155380ebf9fe3: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.6">Jos 12:6</reference> <div eID="gen2831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2832" type="x-p"/> These two kings were smitten by Moses, etc.: vid., Num 21:21., and Num 32:33.
entries.d5d8ae40512a2db8038a38bb273a36dae531260f: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.7-Josh.12.8">Jos 12:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen2832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2833" type="x-p"/> List of the <hi type="italic">thirty-one kings of Canaan</hi> whom Joshua smote on the western side of the Jordan, “<hi type="italic">from Baal-gad, in the valley of Lebanon, to the bald mountain that goeth up towards Seir</hi>” (see <reference osisRef="Josh.11.17">Jos 11:17</reference>). This land Joshua gave to the other tribes of Israel. (On the different parts of the land, see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.1">Jos 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">Jos 10:40</reference>, and Jos 11:2.)
entries.b48f4bd4d67a7e758def4b5262a8b59c5e855c42: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.9-Josh.12.18">Jos 12:9-18</reference> <div eID="gen2833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2834" type="x-p"/> The different kings are given in the order in which they were defeated: Jericho (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.1">Jos 6:1</reference>); Ai (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.2">Jos 7:2</reference>); Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and <hi type="italic">Eglon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.3">Jos 10:3</reference>); Gezer (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.33">Jos 10:33</reference>); and Debir (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.38">Jos 10:38</reference>). Those given in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.12.13">Jos 12:13</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.14">Jos 12:14</reference> are not mentioned by name in Josh 10. <hi type="italic">Geder</hi>, possibly the same as <hi type="italic">Gedor</hi> upon the mountains of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.58">Jos 15:58</reference>), which has been preserved under the old name of <hi type="italic">Jedur</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 186, and Bibl. Res. p. 282). <hi type="italic">Hormah</hi> (i.e., banning) was in the south of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.30">Jos 15:30</reference>), and was allotted to the Simeonites (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.4">Jos 19:4</reference>). It was called <hi type="italic">Zephath</hi> by the Canaanites (Jdg 1:17; see at Num 21:3), was on the southern slope of the mountains of the Amalekites or Amorites, the present ruins of <hi type="italic">Sepâta</hi>, on the western slope of the table-land of <hi type="italic">Rakhma</hi>, two hours and a half to the south-west of Khalasa (Elusa: see <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xiv. p. 1085). <hi type="italic">Arad</hi>, also in the Negeb, has been preserved in Tell <hi type="italic">Arad</hi> (see at Num 21:1). <hi type="italic">Libnah</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.10.29">Jos 10:29</reference>). <hi type="italic">Adullam</hi>, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference> among the towns of the plain between Jarmuth and Socoh, was in the neighbourhood of a large cave in which David took refuge when flying from Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1">1Sa 22:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference>). It was fortified by Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.7">2Ch 11:7</reference>), and is mentioned in 2 Macc. 12:38 as the city of Odollam. The Onomast. describes it as being ten Roman miles to the east of Eleutheropolis; but this is a mistake, though it has not yet been discovered. So far as the situation is concerned, <hi type="italic">Deir Dubbân</hi> would suit very well, a place about two hours to the north of Beit Jibrin, near to a large number of caves in the white limestone, which form a kind of labyrinth, as well as some vaulted grottos (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 353, and <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, Reise, pp. 162-3). <hi type="italic">Makkedah</hi>: possibly <hi type="italic">Summeil</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>). <hi type="italic">Bethel</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Beitin</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Josh.8.17">Jos 8:17</reference>). The situation of the towns which follow in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.17">Jos 12:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.18">Jos 12:18</reference> cannot be determined with certainty, as the names <hi type="italic">Tappuach, Aphek,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hefer</hi> are met with again in different parts of Canaan, and <hi type="italic">Lassaron</hi> does not occur again. But if we observe, that just as from <reference osisRef="Josh.12.10">Jos 12:10</reference> onwards those kings'-towns are first of all enumerated, the capture of which has already been described in Josh 10, and then in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.15">Jos 12:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.16">Jos 12:16</reference> certain other towns are added which had been taken in the war with the Canaanites of the south, so likewise in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.19">Jos 12:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.20">Jos 12:20</reference> the capitals of the allied kings of northern Canaan are given first, and after that the other towns that were taken in the northern war, but had not been mentioned by name in Josh 11: there can be no doubt whatever that the four towns in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.17">Jos 12:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.18">Jos 12:18</reference> are to be classed among the kings'-towns taken in the war with the king of Jerusalem and his allies, and therefore are to be sought for in the south of Canaan and not in the north. Consequently we cannot agree with <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> in identifying <hi type="italic">Tappuach</hi> with <hi type="italic">En-Tappuach</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.7">Jos 17:7</reference>), and looking for it in <hi type="italic">Atûf</hi>, a place to the north-east of Nablus and near the valley of the Jordan; we connect it rather with <hi type="italic">Tappuach</hi> in the lowlands of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.34">Jos 15:34</reference>), though the place itself has not yet been discovered. <hi type="italic">Hefer</hi> again is neither to be identified with Gath-hepher in the tribe of Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.13">Jos 19:13</reference>), nor with <hi type="italic">Chafaraim</hi> in the tribe of Issachar (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.19">Jos 19:19</reference>), but is most probably the capital of the land of <hi type="italic">Hefer </hi>(1Ki 4:10), and to be sought for in the neighbourhood of Socoh in the plain of Judah. <hi type="italic">Aphek</hi> is probably the town of that name not far from Ebenezer (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1">1Sa 4:1</reference>), where the ark was taken by the Philistines, and is most likely to be sought for in the plain of Judah, though not in the village of <hi type="italic">Ahbek</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 343); but it has not yet been traced. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> imagines that it was Aphek near to Jezreel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>), which was situated, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi>, in the neighbourhood of Endor (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>; 1Ki 20:25, 1Ki 20:30); but this Aphek is too far north. <hi type="italic">Lassaron</hi> only occurs here, and hitherto it has been impossible to trace it. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes it to be the place called <hi type="italic">Saruneh</hi>, to the west of the lake of Tiberias, and conjectures that the name has been contracted from Lassaron by aphaeresis of the liquid. This is quite possible, if only we could look for Lassaron so far to the north. <hi type="italic">Bachienne</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi> imagine it to be the village of <hi type="italic">Sharon</hi> in the celebrated plain of that name, between Lydda and Arsuf.
entries.4ba26ed76994b09ce9dd4a930497c294351393b9: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.19-Josh.12.20">Jos 12:19-20</reference> <hi type="italic">Madon, Hezor, Shimron-meron,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Achshaph</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>).
entries.f4b00d8ba783636c96325a307232f8cf3db8cde9: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.21">Jos 12:21</reference> <hi type="italic">Taanach</hi>, which was allotted to the Manassites in the territory of Issachar, and given up to the Levites (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.25">Jos 21:25</reference>), but was not entirely wrested from the Canaanites (Jdg 1:27), is the present Tell <hi type="italic">Taënak</hi>, an hour and a quarter to the south-east of Lejun, a flat hill sown with corn; whilst the old name has been preserved in the small village of Taânak, at the south-eastern foot of the Tell (see <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, i. p. 269, and <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. iii. p. 156). - <hi type="italic">Megiddo</hi>, which was also allotted to the Manassites in the territory of Issachar, though without the Canaanites having been entirely expelled (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>; Jdg 1:27), was fortified by Solomon (1Ki 9:15), and is also well known as the place were Ahaziah died (2Ki 9:27), and where Josiah was beaten and slain by Pharaoh Necho (2Ki 23:29-30; 2Ch 35:20.). <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> has shown that it was preserved in the <hi type="italic">Legio</hi> of a later time, the present <hi type="italic">Lejun</hi> (Pal. iii. pp. 177ff.; see also Bibl. Res. p. 116).
entries.fc87410248e34e1c087076f24a276186698712e2: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.22">Jos 12:22</reference> <hi type="italic">Kedesh</hi>, a Levitical city and city of refuge upon the mountains of Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.37">Jos 19:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.32">Jos 21:32</reference>), the home of Barak (Jdg 4:6), was conquered and depopulated by Tiglath-Pileser (2Ki 15:29), and was also a well-known place after the captivity (1 Macc. 11:61ff.) It is now an insignificant village, still bearing the ancient name, to the north-west of the lake of Huleh, or, according to <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi> (Reise. ii. p. 355), nothing but a miserable farmstead upon a Tell at the south-west extremity of a well-cultivated table-land, with a large quantity of antiquities about, viz., hewn stones, relics of columns, sarcophagi, and two ruins of large buildings, with an open and extensive prospect on every side (see also <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. pp. 367ff.). <hi type="italic">Jokneam</hi>, near <hi type="italic">Carmel</hi>, as a Levitical town in the territory of Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.11">Jos 19:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.34">Jos 21:34</reference>). <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi> and <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (Bibl. Res. p. 114) suppose that they have found it in Tell <hi type="italic">Kaimôn</hi>, on the eastern side of the Wady <hi type="italic">el Milh</hi>, at the north-west end of a chain of hills running towards the south-east; this Tell being 200 feet high, and occupying a very commanding situation, so that it governed the main pass on the western side of Esdraelon towards the southern plain. <hi type="italic">Kaimôn</hi> is the Arabic form of the ancient Καμμωνά, <hi type="italic">Cimana</hi>, which <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> describe in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> as being six Roman miles to the north of <hi type="italic">Legio</hi>, on the road to Ptolemais.
entries.6ffe6be54d30c8c4b47afcb71f2ae151a2e9007d: <reference osisRef="Josh.12.23-Josh.12.24">Jos 12:23-24</reference> <hi type="italic">Dor</hi>: see Jos 11:2. <hi type="italic">Gilgal</hi>: the seat of the king of the <hi type="italic">Goyim</hi> (a proper name, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Gen 14:1</reference>), in all probability the same place as the <hi type="italic">villa nomine Galgulis</hi> mentioned in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v. Gelgel</hi>) as being six Roman miles to the north of Antipatris, which still exists in the Moslem village of <hi type="italic">Jiljule</hi> (now almost a ruin; see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 136), although this village is only two miles E.S.E. of Kefr Sâba, the ancient Antipatris (see <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 568-9). Thirza, the capital of the kings of Israel down to the time of Omri (1Ki 14:17; 1Ki 15:21, 1Ki 15:33; 1Ki 16:6.), is probably the present Talluza, an elevated and beautifully situated place, of a considerable size, surrounded by large olive groves, two hours to the north of Shechem (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 302, and <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, ii. p. 294).  <chapter eID="Josh.12"/> <div eID="gen2834" type="x-p"/>

entries.7b3fdfddb643cbfdc5a1f6d1e3895638d038ed15:
1. NOW these are the kings, etc This chapter does not need a lengthened exposition, as it only enumerates the kings of whose territories the Israelites gained possession. Two of them are beyond the Jordan, Og and Sihon, whose rule was extensive; in the land of Canaan there are thirty-one. But though each of those now summarily mentioned was previously given more in detail, there is very good reason for here placing before our eyes as it were a living picture of the goodness of God, proving that there had been a complete ratification and performance of the covenant made with Abraham as given in the words, “Unto thy seed will I give this land.” (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 13:15; Genesis 15:18) This living image of the grace of God is here set before us as if the reality were actually present.
Latin, “Quam si nos Deus in rem praesentem adduceret.” French, “Comme si Dieu nous mettoit presentement sur le faict, pour nous faire voire la chose de nos yeux;” “As if God were putting us actually upon the spot to make us see the thing with our own eyes.” — Ed.
Joshua was eighty years of age when he entered the land. In this aged man how could there be so much vigor
French, “Comment un povre vieillard pouvoit-il estre si vigoureux;” “How could a poor old man be so vigorous.” — Ed.
as to fit him for carrying on so many wars and enduring the fatigues of warfare, had not celestial virtue furnished him with more than mortal strength? And were not his uninterrupted career of victory, his success under all circumstances, the ease, free from doubt and uncertainty, with which he stormed cities, the rapidity of his movements, and his inflexible firmness — were not all these clear evidences of the hand of God, just as if it had appeared from heaven?
The object of defining the countries by their boundaries was to give a better display of the divine power by setting forth their extent; but this of course was only for those to whom their site was known. Hence, for any one not acquainted with the geography to dwell upon the names, would be vain and foolish curiosity. I admit, indeed, that it is useful to pay attention to the places with which, from their being often mentioned in Scripture, our knowledge ought to be somewhat more familiar, as when the boundaries are fixed by the brook Jabok, in the district of Lebanon and the lake of Gennesaret, here called the Sea of Cineroth, and elsewhere Cinereth. For a slight attention will help us to understand the narrative. If we cannot go farther, let us leave those who are better skilled to give a more searching discussion of what is beyond our reach.
It is evident from these remarks, that though in some other passages Calvin seems to speak rather disparagingly of the elucidation which the Scripture narrative may receive from geography, he did not so much underrate its importance as lament its imperfection at the period when he wrote. All complaint on this head has now been happily removed; and it may safely be affirmed, that nothing has done more to clear up obscurities in the Sacred Volume and triumphantly establish its strict and literal accuracy, then the labors and discoveries of recent travelers.
But although the dominions of these petty kings were narrow and not very populous, we shall however see that many towns were annexed to their principal cities; their number may be ascertained especially from what is said of the lot of the Levites. On the other hand, if we reflect how one small territory could receive and maintain old men, women, and children, nay, a great part of the people with their domestic animals, we cannot fail to admire the inestimable goodness of God which prevented all things from being thrown into complete and irremediable confusion.
Latin, “Ne horribili confusione, omnia miscerentur.” French, “Que tout ne vint a estre brouille pesle mesle d’une confusion horrible;” “That every thing was not hurled pell-mell into horrible confusion.” — Ed.
CHAPTER 13
Joshua 13:1-14
1. Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed.
1. Quum autem senuisset Josue, et venisset in dies, dixit ei Jehova, Tu senuisti, venisti in dies, et multa terra admodum superest ad possidendum.
2. This is the land that yet remaineth: all the borders of the Philistines, and all Geshuri,
2. Haec est terra quae residua est, omnes limites Philisthinorum, et omnis Gessuri.
3. From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites:
3. A Nilo qui est e regione AEgypti usque ad terminum Ecron, qui est ab aquilone, quae Chananeae reputatur, quinque principatus Philisthinorum, Azathaeus, Asdodaeus, Ascalonaeus, Gitthaeus et Ekronaeus et Auaei.
4. From the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that is beside the Sidonians, unto Aphek, to the borders of the Amorites:
4. Ab austro universa terra Chananaei et Meara, quae est Sidoniorum usque ad Paera, usque ad terminum Aemorrhaei.
5. And the land of the Giblites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrising, from Baalgad under mount Hermon unto the entering into Hamath.
5. Et terra Gibli, et totus Libanus ad ortum solis a Baal-gad sub monte Hermon, donec pervenias Hemath.
6. All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon unto Misrephothmaim, and all the Sidonians, them will I drive out from before the children of Israel: only divide thou it by lot unto the Israelites for an inheritance, as I have commanded thee.
6. Omnes habitotores montis a Libano usque ad fervores aquarum: omnes Sidonios ego expellam a facie filiorum Israel: tantum jacias sortem, ut sit in haereditatem Israel, sicut praecepi tibi.
7. Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance unto the nine tribes, and the half tribe of Manasseh;
7. Nunc ergo divide terram istam in haereditatem novem tribubus, et dimidiae tribui Manasse.
8. With whom the Reubenites and the Gadites have received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond Jordan eastward, even as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them;
8. Praeter eam Rubenitae, et Gaditae acceperunt partes suas, quas dedit iis Moses trans Jordanem ad orientem, sicut dedit eis Moses servus Jehovae.
9. From Aroer, that is upon the bank of the river Arnon, and the city that is in the midst of the river, and all the plain of Medeba unto Dibon;
9. Ab Aroer quae est juxta ripam fluminis Arnon, et urbem ipsam quae est in medio vallis, et totam planitiem Medeba usque ad Dibon.
10. And all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, which reigned in Heshbon, unto the border of the children of Ammon;
10. Et omnes urbes Sihon regis Aemorrhaei, qui regnabat in Hesbon, usque ad terminum filiorum Ammon.
11. And Gilead, and the border of the Geshurites and Maachathites, and all mount Hermon, and all Bashan unto Salcah;
11. Et Gilead et terminum Gessuri, et Maachati, et totum montem Hermon, et universum Basan usque ad Salchah.
12. All the kingdom of Og in Bashan, which reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei, who remained of the remnant of the giants: for these did Moses smite, and cast them out.
12. Universum regnum Og in Basan, qui regnabat in Astaroth, et in Edrei: hic supererat ex residuo Rephaim, quos percussit Moses et expulit.
13. Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day.
13. Non expulerunt autem filii Israel Gessuri et Maachati: propterea habitavit Gessur et Maachat in medio Israel usque ad hunc diem.
14. Only unto the tribe of Levi he gave none inheritance; the sacrifices of the LORD God of Israel made by fire are their inheritance, as he said unto them.
14. Tantum tribui Levi non dedit haereditatem, sacrificia Jehovae Dei Israel sunt hereditas ejus, quemadmodum loquutus est de ea.
